Preface
The intent of the System Impact Study is to determine a plan, with approximate cost and construction
time estimates, to connect the subject generation interconnection project to the PJM network at a
location specified by the Interconnection Customer. As a requirement for interconnection, the
Interconnection Customer may be responsible for the cost of constructing: Network Upgrades, which
are facility additions, or upgrades to existing facilities, that are needed to maintain the reliability of the
PJM system. All facilities required for interconnection of a generation interconnection project must be
designed to meet the technical specifications (on PJM web site) for the appropriate transmission owner.
In some instances an Interconnection Customer may not be responsible for 100% of the identified
network upgrade cost because other transmission network uses, e.g. another generation interconnection
or merchant transmission upgrade, may also contribute to the need for the same network reinforcement.
The possibility of sharing the reinforcement costs with other projects may be identified in the
Feasibility Study, but the actual allocation will be deferred until the System Impact Study is performed.
The System Impact Study estimates do not include the feasibility, cost, or time required to obtain
property rights and permits for construction of the required facilities. The project developer is
responsible for the right of way, real estate, and construction permit issues. For properties currently
owned by Transmission Owners, the costs may be included in the study.
Revision from System Impact Study January 2020
The AB2-019 System Impact Study has been revised to reflect the correct Firm Transmission Injection
Rights for the Y3-092 project.
General
ITC Lake Erie Connector, LLC, the Interconnection Customer (IC), has proposed a 28 MW uprate to
their Queue Y3-092 Merchant Transmission line to connect Ontario IESO’s transmission system to
Mid-Atlantic Interstate Transmission’s (or “MAIT”) transmission system, in Erie County, PA. The
installed facilities will have a capability of 1028 MW- with 1028 MW of this output being recognized
by PJM as non-firm Transmission Withdrawal Rights (TWR). The installed facilities will also have a
capability of 1000 MW Firm Transmission Injection Rights (TIR). (See chart below). The proposed
Commercial Operation Date (COD) for this project is March 31, 2024.

Executive Summary
PJM queue project AB2-019 is an interconnection request for a Merchant Transmission line to
connect Ontario IESO’s transmission system to MAIT’s transmission system, in Erie County, PA.
AB2-019 is an uprate to Y3-092, which was a new interconnection request for adding a HVDC
link between Erie West 345 kV substation in the PJM system and Nanticoke 500 kV substation in
the IESO system. After AB2-019 uprate, the HVDC link will be based on ±320 kV, VSC
technology for 1032 MW withdrawal from the IESO system with a net 1000 MW injection into
the PJM system for the import condition and 1028 MW withdrawal from the PJM system for the
export condition from PJM perspective.
Dynamic simulation analysis is required as part of PJM’s Generation and Transmission
Interconnection Process. This Scope of Work describes how the dynamic simulation analysis of
the AB2-019 will be carried out as part of the overall system impact study.
For the import conditions, the HVDC link was set at 1000 MW injection into the PJM system with
the corresponding withdrawal from the IESO’s system. The AC Control Mode for the VSC on
both sides (Nanticoke 500 kV and Erie West 345 kV) was set at voltage.
For the export conditions, the HVDC link was set at 997.7 MW injection into the IESO system
with the corresponding withdrawal (1028 MW) from the PJM system. The AC Control Mode for
the VSC on both sides (Nanticoke 500 kV and Erie West 345 kV) was set at voltage.
This report describes a dynamic simulation analysis of AB2-019 as part of the overall system
impact study.
The load flow scenarios for the analysis were based on the RTEP 2020 Light Load and Summer
Peak case, modified to include applicable queue projects.
The AB2-019 queue project was tested for compliance with NERC, PJM and other applicable
criteria. The range of contingencies evaluated was limited to that necessary to assess compliance
and each was limited to a 20-second simulation time period.
Simulated NERC Standard TPL-001 faults include:
1. Three-phase (3ph) fault with normal clearing (Category P1)
2. Operating of a line section w/o a fault, Single-line-to-ground (slg) on Bus Section and
Breaker. (Category P2)
3. Single-line-to-ground (slg) with delayed clearing as a result of breaker failure (Category
P4)
4. Single-line-to-ground (slg) with delayed clearing as a result of protection failure (Category
P5)
5. Single-line-to-ground (slg) with normal clearing for common structure (Category P7)
Note: For generator interconnection studies, Category P3 and P6 faults will be studied on an as
needed basis. In this study, P2 contingencies are covered by P1 and P4 contingencies.
© PJM Interconnection 2020. All rights reserved 9 AB2-019 “Erie West 345 kV”
The system was tested for a system intact condition and the fault types listed above. Specific
fault descriptions and breaker clearing times used for this study are provided in the result table.
The three phase faults with normal clearing time will also be performed with prior outage of:
a) Erie West - Ashtabula - Perry 345kV line
b) Erie West – Wayne 345kV line
c) Erie West – Erie South 345kV line
d) Armstrong – Homer City 345kV line
e) Wayne – Handsome Shake 345kV line
For all simulations, the queue project under study along with the rest of the PJM system were
required to maintain synchronism and with all states returning to an acceptable new condition
following the disturbance.
For the remaining fault contingencies tested on the 2020 Light Load and Summer Peak case:
a) Post-contingency oscillations were positively damped with a damping margin of at least
3% for all modes.
b) The HVDC was able to ride through all faults.
c) Following fault clearing, all bus voltages recover to a minimum of 0.7 per unit after 2.5
seconds (except where protective action isolates that bus).
d) No transmission element trips, other than those either directly connected or designed to
trip as a consequence of that fault.
No mitigations were found to be required.
